This exercise follows [Geographically Weighted Predictive
Models](https://r4gdsa.netlify.app/chap14.html), the reading for the Geographically
Weighted Predictive Modelling block of the course.

## 1. Overview

Exercise 7 used geographically weighted regression to *explain* condo prices: which
drivers matter, and where. This exercise turns the same idea towards *prediction*:
given a flat's attributes and location, how accurately can its resale price be
estimated, and does letting the model vary over space help?

Four models are compared on HDB resale flats:

1. ordinary multiple linear regression, which assumes one set of coefficients
   everywhere;
2. geographically weighted regression (GWR), which lets those coefficients vary;
3. a random forest, which drops the linear form but still fits one model for the
   whole island;
4. a geographically weighted random forest (GRF), which fits a small random forest
   around every location.

The handout fits all four and reports the test error of only the last. Section 10
fills in the comparison, and section 11 asks whether the test error means what it
appears to mean.

## 2. The Data

The handout supplies one prepared file, `mdata.rds`, built from HDB resale
transactions (Data.gov.sg) joined to locational factors: distance to the CBD, MRT,
parks, malls, hawker centres, eldercare, CHAS clinics, supermarkets and good primary
schools, and counts of kindergartens, childcare centres, bus stops and primary schools
nearby. The raw sources are listed in the handout but not distributed, so I work from
the prepared file. I checked my copy against three independent course repositories;
all three are byte-identical.

## 3. Getting Started

```{r}
pacman::p_load(sf, spdep, GWmodel, SpatialML, ranger,
               tmap, rsample, Metrics, corrplot, tidyverse)
```

The handout calls `corrplot::corrplot()` and `ranger()` without loading either. `ranger`
happens to be attached by `SpatialML`; I load both explicitly so the page does not
depend on that.

### A note on how this page is computed

Several steps take a long time on 10,000 points: the GWR bandwidth search took 16
minutes here, and the geographically weighted random forest considerably longer. Like
the handout, I fit each of them once and save the result as an `.rds` file. Those
chunks are shown with `eval: false`, and the page reads the saved objects. All of them
run from one script, `R/fit_models.R`, which skips any step whose output already
exists.

## 4. Preparing the Data

### 4.1 Reading the data

```{r}
mdata <- read_rds("data/rawdata/mdata.rds")
dim(mdata)
st_crs(mdata)$epsg
```

15,901 transactions with 17 attributes, already projected to SVY21 (EPSG:3414).

```{r}
summary(mdata$resale_price)
```

### 4.2 Training and test sets

```{r}
#| eval: false
set.seed(1234)
resale_split <- initial_split(mdata, prop = 6.5/10,)
train_data <- training(resale_split)
test_data <- testing(resale_split)

write_rds(train_data, "data/model/train_data.rds")
write_rds(test_data, "data/model/test_data.rds")
```

```{r}
train_data <- read_rds("data/model/train_data.rds")
test_data <- read_rds("data/model/test_data.rds")
c(train = nrow(train_data), test = nrow(test_data))
```

A 65/35 random split: 10,335 flats to calibrate on and 5,566 to test against. The
split is random *over flats*. Section 11 shows why that matters.

## 5. Correlation Matrix

```{r}
#| fig-height: 7
mdata_nogeo <- mdata %>% st_drop_geometry()
corrplot::corrplot(cor(mdata_nogeo[, 2:17]),
                   diag = FALSE,
                   order = "AOE",
                   tl.pos = "td",
                   tl.cex = 0.5,
                   method = "number",
                   type = "upper")
```

No pair of predictors is correlated above 0.8, so there is no case for dropping any of
them. As Exercise 7 showed, that global check says nothing about collinearity inside
a GWR neighbourhood, but for prediction rather than interpretation it matters less: a
collinear local model can still predict well even when its individual coefficients
cannot be trusted.

## 6. Multiple Linear Regression

```{r}
#| eval: false
price_mlr <- lm(resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm +
                  storey_order + remaining_lease_mths +
                  PROX_CBD + PROX_ELDERLYCARE + PROX_HAWKER +
                  PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK + PROX_MALL +
                  PROX_SUPERMARKET + WITHIN_350M_KINDERGARTEN +
                  WITHIN_350M_CHILDCARE + WITHIN_350M_BUS +
                  WITHIN_1KM_PRISCH,
                data = train_data)
write_rds(price_mlr, "data/model/price_mlr.rds")
```

```{r}
price_mlr <- read_rds("data/model/price_mlr.rds")
summary(price_mlr)
```

The linear model explains 74% of the variance in resale price on the training data.
Every predictor is significant. The signs mostly read sensibly: price falls with
distance from the CBD and from the MRT, and rises with floor area, storey and remaining
lease, about S$345 for every extra month of lease.

## 7. Geographically Weighted Regression

### 7.1 Adaptive bandwidth

```{r}
#| eval: false
bw_adaptive <- bw.gwr(
  formula = resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm +
    storey_order + remaining_lease_mths +
    PROX_CBD + PROX_ELDERLYCARE + PROX_HAWKER +
    PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK + PROX_MALL +
    PROX_SUPERMARKET + WITHIN_350M_KINDERGARTEN +
    WITHIN_350M_CHILDCARE + WITHIN_350M_BUS +
    WITHIN_1KM_PRISCH,
  data = train_data,
  approach = "CV",
  kernel = "gaussian",
  adaptive = TRUE,
  longlat = FALSE)
write_rds(bw_adaptive, "data/model/bw_adaptive.rds")
```

```{r}
bw_adaptive <- read_rds("data/model/bw_adaptive.rds")
bw_adaptive
```

Cross-validation selects 40 nearest neighbours, the same as the handout.

### 7.2 Calibrating the GWR model

```{r}
#| eval: false
gwr_adaptive <- gwr.basic(
  formula = resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm +
    storey_order + remaining_lease_mths +
    PROX_CBD + PROX_ELDERLYCARE +
    PROX_HAWKER + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK +
    PROX_MALL + PROX_SUPERMARKET +
    WITHIN_350M_KINDERGARTEN +
    WITHIN_350M_CHILDCARE +
    WITHIN_350M_BUS + WITHIN_1KM_PRISCH,
  data = train_data,
  bw = bw_adaptive,
  kernel = "gaussian",
  adaptive = TRUE,
  longlat = FALSE)
write_rds(gwr_adaptive, "data/model/gwr_adaptive.rds")
```

```{r}
gwr_adaptive <- read_rds("data/model/gwr_adaptive.rds")
gwr_adaptive$GW.diagnostic[c("AICc", "gw.R2", "gwR2.adj", "enp")] %>% unlist() %>% round(4)
```

I print the diagnostics rather than the whole object, which runs to several screens
of coefficient summaries. GWR raises R² on the training data from 0.74 to 0.97 and
lowers AICc by about 18,000, at the cost of roughly 1,730 effective parameters. That is
the in-sample picture. Whether the extra flexibility carries over to flats the model
has not seen is the question of section 10.

### 7.3 Predicting the test set

The handout predicts with `gwr.predict()`:

```{r}
#| eval: false
gwr_pred <- gwr.predict(
  formula = resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm +
    storey_order + remaining_lease_mths +
    PROX_CBD + PROX_ELDERLYCARE + PROX_HAWKER +
    PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK + PROX_MALL +
    PROX_SUPERMARKET + WITHIN_350M_KINDERGARTEN +
    WITHIN_350M_CHILDCARE + WITHIN_350M_BUS +
    WITHIN_1KM_PRISCH,
  data = train_data,
  predictdata = test_data,
  bw = 40,
  kernel = "gaussian",
  adaptive = TRUE,
  longlat = FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-important}
## `gwr.predict()` does not work at this size in GWmodel 2.4.1

**It fails.** Run as written, the call stops with `No regression point is fixed`. The
cause is a bug in the package. When the training set has more than 5,000 points,
`gwr.predict()` stops precomputing distances and calls
`gw.dist(fd.locat, focus = i, p, theta, longlat)` inside a loop. Those arguments are
positional, so `p` (the Minkowski power, 2) lands in the `rp.locat` slot and the
function finds one "regression point" where it asked for point `i`. With 10,335
training flats the broken branch is always taken. The handout's version of GWmodel
evidently did not have this problem.

**The obvious workaround is impractical.** Passing both distance matrices (`dMat1`,
`dMat2`) skips the broken branch. But the function then goes on to compute a
prediction *variance*, which needs `t(I - S) %*% (I - S)` for a 10,335 by 10,335 hat
matrix `S`: several dense matrices of about 850 MB each and roughly a trillion
floating-point operations. On this machine it ran for over an hour without finishing.

**What I do instead.** A GWR prediction is the local coefficients at the test
location, calibrated on the training flats, multiplied by the test flat's attributes.
`gwr.basic()` with `regression.points` returns exactly those coefficients and skips
the variance, so the whole step takes about 30 seconds:
:::

```{r}
#| eval: false
gwr_at_test <- gwr.basic(
  formula = resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm +
    storey_order + remaining_lease_mths +
    PROX_CBD + PROX_ELDERLYCARE + PROX_HAWKER +
    PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK + PROX_MALL +
    PROX_SUPERMARKET + WITHIN_350M_KINDERGARTEN +
    WITHIN_350M_CHILDCARE + WITHIN_350M_BUS +
    WITHIN_1KM_PRISCH,
  data = train_data,
  regression.points = test_data,
  bw = 40,
  kernel = "gaussian",
  adaptive = TRUE,
  longlat = FALSE)

B <- as.matrix(st_drop_geometry(st_as_sf(gwr_at_test$SDF))[, 1:15])
X <- cbind(1, as.matrix(st_drop_geometry(test_data)[, all.vars(formula(price_mlr))[-1]]))
gwr_pred <- tibble(prediction = rowSums(B * X))
write_rds(gwr_pred, "data/model/gwr_pred.rds")
```

To be sure this is the same model and not a near relative, `R/check_gwr_predict.R`
runs both on a subset small enough for `gwr.predict()` to finish (3,000 training flats,
400 test flats):

```{r}
read_rds("data/model/gwr_predict_check.rds")
```

The two sets of predictions are identical. The only thing given up is the
prediction variance, which the handout does not use.

The handout also computes a separate adaptive bandwidth on the *test* data and saves
it, then predicts with a hard-coded `bw = 40`. That bandwidth is never used, and it
should not be: choosing a bandwidth on the test set would let the test data shape the
model it is meant to judge. I leave it out.

## 8. Random Forest

### 8.1 Coordinates and geometry

```{r}
coords_train <- st_coordinates(train_data)
coords_test <- st_coordinates(test_data)

train_data_nogeom <- train_data %>% st_drop_geometry()
test_data_nogeom <- test_data %>% st_drop_geometry()
```

### 8.2 A non-spatial random forest

```{r}
#| eval: false
set.seed(1234)
rf <- ranger(
  formula = resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm +
    storey_order + remaining_lease_mths +
    PROX_CBD + PROX_ELDERLYCARE +
    PROX_HAWKER + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK +
    PROX_MALL + PROX_SUPERMARKET +
    WITHIN_350M_KINDERGARTEN +
    WITHIN_350M_CHILDCARE +
    WITHIN_350M_BUS +
    WITHIN_1KM_PRISCH,
  data = train_data_nogeom)
write_rds(rf, "data/model/rf.rds")
```

```{r}
rf <- read_rds("data/model/rf.rds")
rf
```

The out-of-bag R² is 0.9494, against the handout's 0.9496; the trees are random, and the handout's ranger version draws them slightly differently. Out-of-bag
error is the random forest's built-in estimate of test error: each tree is scored on
the flats it did not sample. Its square root, about S$27,000, is a figure to keep in
mind for section 10.

## 9. Geographically Weighted Random Forest

### 9.1 Calibrating

```{r}
#| eval: false
set.seed(1234)
gwRF_adaptive <- grf(
  formula = resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm +
    storey_order + remaining_lease_mths +
    PROX_CBD + PROX_ELDERLYCARE +
    PROX_HAWKER + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK +
    PROX_MALL + PROX_SUPERMARKET +
    WITHIN_350M_KINDERGARTEN +
    WITHIN_350M_CHILDCARE +
    WITHIN_350M_BUS + WITHIN_1KM_PRISCH,
  dframe = train_data_nogeom,
  bw = 40,
  kernel = "adaptive",
  coords = coords_train)
write_rds(gwRF_adaptive, "data/model/gwRF_adaptive.rds")
```

`grf()` fits one global random forest and then, for every training flat, a local
forest on its 40 nearest neighbours. That is 10,335 small forests, which is why this
step is slow.

### 9.2 Predicting the test set

```{r}
#| eval: false
gwRF_adaptive <- read_rds("data/model/gwRF_adaptive.rds")
test_data_nogeom <- cbind(test_data, coords_test) %>%
  st_drop_geometry()

gwRF_pred <- predict(gwRF_adaptive,
                         test_data_nogeom,
                         x.var.name = "X",
                         y.var.name = "Y",
                         local.w = 1,
                         global.w = 0)
write_rds(gwRF_pred, "data/model/GRF_pred.rds")
```

The handout calls `predict.grf()` directly. SpatialML 1.8.2 no longer exports it; it
is now an S3 method for the `grf` class, so the generic `predict()` reaches the same
function.

`local.w = 1, global.w = 0` means each test flat is predicted entirely by the local
forest of its nearest training location, with no weight on the global forest.

```{r}
GRF_pred <- read_rds("data/model/GRF_pred.rds")
test_data_p <- cbind(test_data, GRF_pred = GRF_pred) %>%
  select(resale_price, GRF_pred)
rmse(test_data_p$resale_price, test_data_p$GRF_pred)
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4.5
ggplot(test_data_p, aes(x = GRF_pred, y = resale_price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, size = 0.8) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "#137C8B") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = "Predicted by GRF (S$)", y = "Actual resale price (S$)")
```

My GRF test RMSE is S$28,180, within S$20 of the handout's S$28,161. The small gap is
expected: `grf()` grows thousands of random trees, and its internal random-number use
differs slightly across package versions. The scatterplot sits tightly on the
diagonal for most flats and fans out above about S$500,000, where transactions are sparse
and each local forest has few comparable sales to learn from.

## 10. Comparing All Four Models on the Same Test Set

The handout reports the GRF's test error and stops. A test error means little alone;
the question a predictive modelling exercise has to answer is which model to use.

```{r}
gwr_pred <- read_rds("data/model/gwr_pred.rds")

preds <- tibble(
  actual = test_data$resale_price,
  MLR = predict(price_mlr, test_data),
  GWR = gwr_pred$prediction,
  `Random forest` = predict(rf, test_data_nogeom)$predictions,
  GRF = GRF_pred)

comparison <- preds %>%
  pivot_longer(-actual, names_to = "model", values_to = "pred") %>%
  group_by(model) %>%
  summarise(RMSE = rmse(actual, pred),
            MAE = mae(actual, pred),
            MAPE_pct = 100 * mape(actual, pred)) %>%
  arrange(RMSE) %>%
  mutate(across(c(RMSE, MAE), round), MAPE_pct = round(MAPE_pct, 2))
comparison
```

::: {.callout-note}
## On this split, plain GWR is the best model and the GRF is the weakest of the three spatial ones

**GWR wins on every measure**: RMSE S$24,800, MAE S$17,900, 4.2% mean absolute
percentage error. The plain random forest comes second (S$26,500), and the
geographically weighted random forest third (S$28,200). Linear regression is far
behind at S$61,000, more than twice the error of any other model.

**The GRF is not an improvement on a plain random forest here.** It is the model the
handout builds towards, and on this test set it is worse than the simpler forest it
extends. Two settings explain most of it. Each local forest is trained on only 40
flats, and `local.w = 1` throws away the global forest entirely. A forest grown on 40
observations is a weak learner, and a weighted mix of local and global (for example
`local.w = 0.5`) is the usual remedy in the GRF literature.

**GWR wins in every price band**, not just on average:

| | bottom half | 50th to 90th percentile | top 10% |
|---|---|---|---|
| GWR | 20,091 | 25,499 | 39,194 |
| Random forest | 21,135 | 25,832 | 46,380 |
| GRF | 22,616 | 29,277 | 44,289 |
| MLR | 49,119 | 57,823 | 108,638 |

*RMSE in S$ by actual price band, computed from the same predictions.*

So "machine learning beats regression" is not the lesson. "Letting the model vary
over space beats not letting it" is, and the linear form, once it is local, is
competitive with the forest.
:::

## 11. What the Random Split Hides

### 11.1 Most test flats have a twin in the training set

HDB flats come in blocks. A block has dozens of flats at one address, and `mdata`
gives every flat in a block the same coordinates and the same locational
attributes. A random split over flats therefore sends some of a block's flats to
training and others to test.

```{r}
H <- read_rds("data/model/holdout.rds")
H$leak
```

**`r round(100 * H$leak$same_location)`%** of test flats have a training flat at
exactly the same coordinates, and `r round(100 * H$leak$within_100m)`% have one within
100 m. For those flats, predicting the price is close to looking it up: a flexible
model only has to recognise the block and read off what similar flats in it sold for.
That is a legitimate task, valuing a flat in a block that has recent sales, but it is
not the same as predicting a price where the model has no local evidence.

### 11.2 A spatially blocked holdout

To separate the two, `R/spatial_holdout.R` divides Singapore into 2 km grid cells and
sends whole cells to the test set, so no test flat has a training flat in its own
neighbourhood. It repeats this for five random draws of held-out cells, for the three
models that are fast enough to refit: linear regression, the random forest, and GWR
(keeping the 40-neighbour bandwidth from section 7).

```{r}
H$blocked %>% mutate(across(c(median_nn_m, MLR, RF, GWR), round))
```

```{r}
# Medians rather than means across the five draws: one GWR draw fails badly
# (discussed below) and a mean would be that one draw.
blocked_median <- H$blocked %>% summarise(across(c(MLR, RF, GWR), median))
random_rmse <- setNames(comparison$RMSE, comparison$model)

tibble(model = c("MLR", "Random forest", "GWR"),
       `random split RMSE` = unname(random_rmse[c("MLR", "Random forest", "GWR")]),
       `spatially blocked RMSE (median of 5)` =
         round(c(blocked_median$MLR, blocked_median$RF, blocked_median$GWR))) %>%
  mutate(ratio = round(`spatially blocked RMSE (median of 5)` / `random split RMSE`, 2))
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Most of the flexible models' advantage is the leak

**Linear regression barely notices the change.** Its error moves from S$61,000 on the
random split to a median of S$62,200 on the blocked one. It never relied on knowing the
block.

**The random forest's error more than doubles**, from S$26,500 to a median of
S$58,100, and in two of the five draws it is worse than linear regression. A forest
predicting a flat whose block it has seen is close to an expert valuer; predicting a
flat in a neighbourhood it has never seen, it is only slightly better than a
regression line.

**GWR's error also more than doubles** (median S$59,500), and in draw 3 it fails
outright: RMSE S$1.5 million. That is not most flats. In that draw, 77 of 5,492 test
flats have errors above S$1 million while the median error is an ordinary S$37,700.
The worst cases are not far from training data (about 200 m), so this is not simple
extrapolation in space. It is the local regression being badly conditioned: when the
40 nearest training flats come from one or two blocks, their locational variables are
nearly identical, the local coefficients become enormous and unstable, and a test flat
whose values differ even slightly is extrapolated wildly. It is the local
collinearity of Exercise 7, showing up as prediction error. A random forest cannot
fail this way, because its predictions are averages of observed prices.

**What the comparison in section 10 actually measured.** On the random split, the
three spatial models are being rewarded mostly for recognising blocks they have
already seen. That is a legitimate use case (valuing a flat in a block with recent
sales) and for that use GWR is the best of the four. For valuing flats where the model
has no nearby evidence, a new estate or a block with no recent sales, none of the
flexible models is much better than linear regression, and GWR needs guarding
against its rare catastrophic predictions. The geographically weighted random forest
is not included here because each refit takes about nine minutes; I would expect it to
lose its advantage in the same way.
:::

## 12. What I Take From This Exercise

**The handout's comparison was missing its comparison.** It builds four models and
reports the test error of one. Scored on the same test set, plain GWR is the most
accurate (RMSE S$24,800), ahead of the random forest (S$26,500) and the geographically
weighted random forest (S$28,200), with linear regression far behind (S$61,000). The
model the exercise builds towards came third of the four.

**A random split is the wrong test for spatial prediction.** 82% of test flats have a
training flat at the same coordinates, because flats in a block share an address.
Holding out whole 2 km areas instead roughly doubles the error of every flexible
model and leaves linear regression almost unchanged. Which split is right depends on
the question: valuing a flat in a block with recent sales, or valuing one where there
are none. The handout's split answers only the first, and does not say so.

**GWR's local flexibility has a failure mode that forests do not.** Under the blocked
split, one draw produced errors of millions of dollars for a few dozen flats, from
ill-conditioned local regressions. A random forest's prediction is bounded by the
prices it has seen; a local linear model's is not. Anyone deploying GWR for prediction
should clip predictions or check local condition numbers first.

**Two package changes broke the handout as written, silently or not.** `gwr.predict()`
fails for more than 5,000 training points in GWmodel 2.4.1, and its workaround is
computationally impractical because of a prediction variance the exercise never
uses. `predict.grf()` is no longer exported by SpatialML 1.8.2. Neither is a
statistical problem, but both are the kind of thing that makes a reproducible pipeline
stop being reproducible a year later.

**Connecting back to Exercise 7.** There, local collinearity was a reason not to
interpret individual GWR coefficients. Here it turns out to matter for prediction
too, but only when the model is asked to predict away from the evidence it was fitted
on, which is exactly when a prediction is most useful.

- Roberts, D. R. et al. (2017). Cross-validation strategies for data with temporal, spatial, hierarchical, or phylogenetic structure. *Ecography*, 40(8), 913-929.
